moments.title: The Division of Labour in Society
moments.body:
Durkheim distinguishes mechanical solidarity (similarity-based) from organic solidarity (interdependence-based).

He argues modern societies cohere through specialised, mutually dependent roles.
moments.takeaway: Modernity needs a sociology because it produces a new kind of social bond.

moments.title: Le Suicide
moments.body:
Durkheim shows suicide rates correlate with religion, marital status and wartime, arguing the phenomenon is a 'social fact'.

Later critics (Douglas, 1967) question whether 19th-century coronial records are robust enough to support the analysis.

quote.text: There can be no sociology unless societies exist, and societies cannot exist if there are only individuals.

moments.takeaway: Sociology stakes its independence from psychology by showing patterns no individual story explains.

moments.title: The Elementary Forms of Religious Life
moments.body: Durkheim treats religion as society's reflection on itself, drawing on Aboriginal Australian ethnography (which he himself never conducted).
moments.takeaway: Foundational theory in sociology often relied on second-hand ethnographic sources.

now.title: Sociology of the social bond today
now.body: Contemporary scholars use Durkheimian frameworks to study loneliness, online community and political polarisation. Suicide research integrates sociological and clinical data.
now.open_questions: How do digital platforms reshape integration and regulation? Are anomic conditions identifiable in contemporary data?

items.reflection: Durkheim wrote during the founding of the French Republic; his concerns about social cohesion echo current public debates.

moments.title: The Communist Manifesto
moments.body: Written in London on the eve of Europe's 1848 revolutions, the pamphlet sketches a theory of history as class struggle.
moments.takeaway: Sociological theory and revolutionary politics emerge intertwined.

moments.title: Capital, volume one
moments.body:
Marx analyses commodity exchange, surplus value and the accumulation of capital using British factory data.

Volumes two and three are published posthumously by Engels.
moments.takeaway: Long-form economic analysis grounded Marx's broader sociological framework.

moments.title: Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century
moments.body: Piketty's long-run tax data reopen debates about capital accumulation and inequality, arguing that returns on capital tend to outpace economic growth.
moments.takeaway: Empirical revival of classical questions can reshape contemporary political debate.

now.title: Class analysis today
now.body: Modern stratification research uses occupational, cultural and wealth measures (e.g. Savage et al.'s 2013 'Great British Class Survey'). Wealth taxation is debated in OECD countries.
now.open_questions: How should new asset categories (housing, pensions, digital) be incorporated into class measures? Does globalisation alter class formation?

items.reflection: Marx's predictions about industrial proletariat formation took unexpected paths in different national contexts.

moments.title: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
moments.body:
Weber links the Calvinist concept of the 'calling' to dispositions favourable to capital accumulation in Northern Europe.

His comparative method ranges across world religions.
moments.takeaway: Religion shapes economic behaviour in ways material analysis alone misses.

moments.title: Economy and Society
moments.body: Compiled after Weber's death in 1920, this massive treatise sets out his typologies of authority (traditional, charismatic, legal-rational) and the analysis of bureaucracy.
moments.takeaway: Bureaucratic rationality, for Weber, was both efficient and dehumanising.

now.title: Rationalisation today
now.body: Weber's themes recur in studies of algorithmic management, performance metrics and credentialism. The 'iron cage' metaphor is used to describe contemporary digital and managerial environments.
now.open_questions: Do algorithmic systems extend or transform bureaucratic rationality? Where do charismatic dynamics arise inside legal-rational structures?

items.reflection: Weber's ambivalence about modernity, both admiring and critical, remains a model for sociological writing.

moments.title: Park and Burgess at Chicago
moments.body:
Robert Park, a former journalist, joins Chicago and develops 'human ecology' as a way to study the city.

The department becomes a centre of empirical urban research.
moments.takeaway: The city itself becomes a laboratory for sociological method.

moments.title: The City
moments.body:
The volume sets out concentric-zone theory of urban growth.

Direct-observation studies by graduate students (Thrasher's The Gang, 1927; Wirth's The Ghetto, 1928) populate the framework.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical models gained empirical bite through ethnographic detail.

moments.title: Street Corner Society
moments.body: Whyte's 'Cornerville' study of an Italian-American Boston neighbourhood becomes a methodological landmark in participant observation.
moments.takeaway: Sustained immersion produced descriptions impossible from a survey.

now.title: Urban ethnography today
now.body: Modern urban ethnographers (e.g. Sudhir Venkatesh, Mitchell Duneier) extend the Chicago tradition. Mixed-methods designs combine ethnography with administrative data.
now.open_questions: What protections should ethnographers offer subjects in surveillance-rich environments? How should AI-assisted coding be used?

items.reflection: Many Chicago School studies treated immigrant and Black communities as objects of study without fully engaging with researchers from those communities.

moments.title: Le Deuxieme Sexe
moments.body:
Beauvoir argues 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', framing gender as constructed.

The book influences both philosophy and what would become feminist sociology.
moments.takeaway: Continental philosophy seeded sociological frameworks decades before they entered the discipline.

moments.title: The Sociology of Housework
moments.body: Oakley's interview study of London housewives establishes domestic labour as a topic for sociology in its own right.
moments.takeaway: Naming unpaid labour as 'work' reshaped how the economy was measured.

moments.title: Crenshaw on intersectionality
moments.body: Crenshaw's legal-theoretical concept of intersectionality is published, eventually reshaping social science measurement.
moments.takeaway: Categories that work singly may obscure compound experiences of inequality.

now.title: Gender sociology today
now.body: Contemporary work combines feminist theory with administrative-data analysis (e.g. gender pay gap research). Time-use surveys measure unpaid labour systematically.
now.open_questions: How are gendered patterns shifting in remote-work economies? How should sex/gender categories be operationalised across heterogeneous populations?

items.reflection: Sociology's gender turn took decades to reorganise curricula, even after the underlying scholarship was established.

moments.title: The Philosophy of Money
moments.body: Simmel analyses how money mediates social relations, freeing individuals from personal dependence while creating new forms of impersonality.
moments.takeaway: Money is not just an economic instrument but a social form.

moments.title: The Metropolis and Mental Life
moments.body: Simmel's essay describes the blase attitude of the urban individual, overstimulated by crowds, advertising and time discipline.

quote.text: The metropolis exacts from man as a discriminating creature a different amount of consciousness than does rural life.

moments.takeaway: Urban experience produces distinctive psychological adaptations.

moments.title: Soziologie
moments.body: Simmel sets out a formal sociology of interaction, focused on dyads, triads, strangers and secrets.
moments.takeaway: Microsocial forms can structure macro phenomena.

now.title: Simmel in urban studies
now.body: Simmel's essay remains a touchstone for urban sociology, digital sociology and studies of attention.
now.open_questions: Does the smartphone intensify Simmel's blase attitude or invert it?

items.reflection: Simmel never received a full professorship in his lifetime; his influence grew through essays read by students of greater names.

moments.title: The City essay
moments.body: Park's programmatic essay proposes the city as a laboratory for sociology, drawing on his journalist background.
moments.takeaway: Treating the city as a laboratory founded an empirical research programme.

moments.title: The City book
moments.body: The book introduces Burgess's concentric-zone model of urban growth, with the central business district, zone of transition, working-class housing, residential and commuter zones.
moments.takeaway: A diagram organised half a century of urban research.

moments.title: Urbanism as a Way of Life
moments.body: Wirth's paper defines urbanism through size, density and heterogeneity, integrating Simmel's themes into Chicago's framework.
moments.takeaway: Definitions shape research agendas.

now.title: Chicago beyond Chicago
now.body: Burgess's diagram has been heavily criticised but remains a teaching staple. Gentrification, sun-belt growth and gated communities have reconfigured urban sociology.
now.open_questions: Do digital labour markets produce new spatial patterns or dissolve them?

items.reflection: The Chicago School made fieldwork central to American sociology and trained a generation of urban ethnographers.

moments.title: The Structure of Social Action
moments.body: Parsons synthesises Durkheim, Weber, Pareto and Marshall into a 'voluntaristic theory of action', introducing them to anglophone sociology.
moments.takeaway: A grand synthesis introduces a generation to its predecessors.

moments.title: The Social System
moments.body: Parsons develops a systems-theoretic account of social order, with pattern variables and functional prerequisites.
moments.takeaway: Functional theory aimed at full generality.

moments.title: Family, Socialization and Interaction Process
moments.body: Parsons and Bales analyse the nuclear family in terms of instrumental and expressive roles.
moments.takeaway: Functionalist family theory carried strong gendered assumptions.

now.title: After Parsons
now.body: Parsonsian functionalism declined under conflict-theory and interpretive critique. Neofunctionalists (Alexander) have partially rehabilitated his thinking.
now.open_questions: What does systems theory contribute to climate and ecological sociology?

items.reflection: Parsons dominated American sociology in the 1950s as much as anyone has dominated a discipline.

moments.title: Social Structure and Anomie
moments.body: Merton extends Durkheim's anomie to American deviance: conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism and rebellion as responses to means-ends strain.
moments.takeaway: Strain theory linked structure to deviant adaptations.

moments.title: Social Theory and Social Structure
moments.body: Merton introduces middle-range theory and the manifest/latent function distinction.
moments.takeaway: Middle-range theory bridged abstract theory and empirical research.

moments.title: Expanded edition
moments.body: The expanded edition consolidates the impact of middle-range theory across American sociology.
moments.takeaway: Editions can mark when a theoretical idea has become institutional.

now.title: Strain and middle-range theory
now.body: Strain theory is still taught in criminology. Middle-range theorising is the implicit standard for most contemporary empirical sociology.
now.open_questions: What contemporary forms of innovation or retreatism does strain theory illuminate?

items.reflection: Merton's framing of theory choices shaped how American sociology defined its own practice.

moments.title: Gramsci arrested
moments.body: Antonio Gramsci, leader of the Italian Communist Party, is arrested by Mussolini's regime.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical work can be done under imprisonment.

moments.title: Prison Notebooks begun
moments.body: Gramsci begins the notebooks that develop hegemony, organic intellectuals and the war of position.
moments.takeaway: Hegemony reframes domination as substantially consensual.

moments.title: Selections published in English
moments.body: Gramsci enters anglophone cultural studies and political theory via the Selections from the Prison Notebooks.
moments.takeaway: Translation timing determines a thinker's audience.

now.title: Hegemony in cultural studies
now.body: Stuart Hall and Birmingham cultural studies built modern uses of hegemony. The concept is invoked in critiques of media, education and global politics.
now.open_questions: What counts as a counter-hegemonic project in fragmented digital media?

items.reflection: Gramsci's notebooks were almost lost; their survival and translation reshaped the Western Marxist tradition.

moments.title: Institute for Social Research founded
moments.body: The Institute is founded with a commitment to Marxist social analysis and interdisciplinary research.
moments.takeaway: Institutional investment can build a theoretical tradition.

moments.title: Dialectic of Enlightenment
moments.who: Adorno and Horkheimer, exile in California
moments.body: The book argues that instrumental reason produces both fascism and the culture industry. Written during exile from Nazism.
moments.takeaway: Critical theory diagnosed modernity from within its catastrophe.

moments.title: The Authoritarian Personality
moments.body: An empirical study uses the F-scale to link personality structure to fascism-receptive attitudes.
moments.takeaway: Frankfurt theorists used quantitative methods as well as critique.

now.title: Critical theory today
now.body: Habermas's communicative action and Honneth's recognition continue the Frankfurt tradition. Algorithmic culture revives 'culture industry' debates.
now.open_questions: Do platform recommender systems constitute a new culture industry?

items.reflection: Frankfurt critical theory developed under emergency conditions of fascism, war and exile.

moments.title: For Marx and Reading Capital
moments.body: Althusser's structuralist Marxism distinguishes scientific from ideological Marx.
moments.takeaway: Structuralism reshaped what counted as Marxist theory.

moments.title: Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses
moments.body: Althusser distinguishes repressive and ideological state apparatuses, theorising how ideology 'interpellates' subjects.
moments.takeaway: Schools, media and family become primary sites of ideology.

moments.title: Althusser kills his wife
moments.body: In November 1980 Althusser strangles his wife Helene Rytmann during a psychiatric episode and is committed.
moments.takeaway: Reception of a theorist sometimes turns on biographical catastrophe.

now.title: Althusser in education theory
now.body: Althusser's account of education as an ISA influences sociology of education and cultural studies.
now.open_questions: What ideological apparatus operates through platform algorithms?

items.reflection: Althusser's influence persisted despite later biographical and intellectual collapse.

moments.title: Mind, Self and Society
moments.body: Mead's lectures, published after his death, develop the I-and-me distinction and role-taking as foundations of selfhood.
moments.takeaway: The self emerges from social interaction.

moments.title: Symbolic interactionism coined
moments.body: Blumer names the tradition descended from Mead and Cooley, emphasising meanings constructed in interaction.
moments.takeaway: A name can consolidate a loose tradition.

moments.title: Symbolic Interactionism
moments.body: Blumer's book lays out the methodological principles: people act towards things on the basis of meanings they hold for them.
moments.takeaway: Methodological commitments shape what counts as data.

now.title: Interactionism today
now.body: Symbolic interactionism underpins much qualitative sociology, from microsociology to ethnography of work.
now.open_questions: How is selfhood constructed in interaction mediated by social media platforms?

items.reflection: American pragmatism gave sociology its strongest interactionist tradition.

moments.title: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
moments.body: Goffman uses dramaturgy to analyse face-to-face interaction as managed performance, with front stage and back stage.

quote.text: All the world is not, of course, a stage, but the crucial ways in which it isn't are not easy to specify.

moments.takeaway: Routine interaction is structured performance.

moments.title: Asylums
moments.body: Asylums analyses total institutions through fieldwork in St Elizabeth's psychiatric hospital, with the moral career of the mental patient.
moments.takeaway: Total institutions strip and remake identity.

moments.title: Stigma
moments.body: Goffman's Stigma analyses spoiled identity and its management, with implications for disability and minority sociology.
moments.takeaway: Identity work is shaped by social discrediting.

now.title: Goffman online
now.body: Goffman's dramaturgy is widely applied to social media impression management, dating apps and influencer self-presentation.
now.open_questions: What happens to the front stage / back stage distinction in always-on platforms?

items.reflection: Goffman's books remain among the most readable in modern sociology.

moments.title: Family and Kinship in East London
moments.body: Their Bethnal Green study documents dense extended kinship networks in a working-class East End community.
moments.takeaway: Empirical sociology challenged assumptions about family decline.

moments.title: The Symmetrical Family
moments.body: Young and Willmott argue post-war affluence is producing more symmetrical conjugal relationships across classes.
moments.takeaway: Family forms shift with economic conditions.

moments.title: The Sociology of Housework
moments.body: Oakley's interviews with 40 London housewives find domestic labour experienced as monotonous and isolating, despite affluence.
moments.takeaway: Feminist critique punctured the symmetrical-family thesis.

now.title: Family sociology today
now.body: Contemporary research addresses cohabitation, same-sex families, transnational families and care chains.
now.open_questions: What counts as a household when housing costs force adult children to remain at home?

items.reflection: Young and Willmott's institute (the Institute of Community Studies) shaped UK family sociology for decades.

moments.title: Family, Socialization and Interaction Process
moments.body: Parsons describes the nuclear family as 'isolated' and specialising in primary socialisation and stabilisation of adult personalities.
moments.takeaway: Functionalism cast the nuclear family as adapted to industrial society.

moments.title: Critiques begin
moments.body: Empirical studies document continued extended-family ties, challenging Parsons's isolation thesis.
moments.takeaway: Empirical work qualifies grand theory.

moments.title: Sex, Gender and Society
moments.body: Oakley distinguishes sex (biological) from gender (cultural), challenging functionalist accounts of gendered roles.
moments.takeaway: Feminist sociology reshaped how the family was theorised.

now.title: Family diversity
now.body: Single-parent, blended, same-sex, and chosen families are central to modern sociology of personal life (Carol Smart).
now.open_questions: How do gender, work and care reconfigure as families diversify?

items.reflection: The 'standard' nuclear family is a brief mid-20th-century arrangement.

moments.title: Sex, Gender and Society
moments.body: Oakley distinguishes sex from gender and challenges biological accounts of feminine roles.
moments.takeaway: Conceptual clarification reshaped feminist sociology.

moments.title: The Sociology of Housework
moments.body: Oakley interviews 40 London housewives and finds dissatisfaction with isolation and monotony, despite material progress.
moments.takeaway: Domestic labour received sociological visibility.

moments.title: Subject Women
moments.body: Oakley advocates for explicitly feminist methodology, treating interviewees as partners rather than data.
moments.takeaway: Method itself becomes a feminist issue.

now.title: Care and labour
now.body: Time-use surveys, care chains and the second-shift hypothesis (Hochschild) extend Oakley's analysis.
now.open_questions: How does remote work reshape the household division of labour?

items.reflection: Oakley combined activist and academic agendas in mid-20th-century British feminist sociology.

moments.title: The Inheritors
moments.body: Bourdieu and Passeron analyse how French universities reproduce class privilege through cultural capital.
moments.takeaway: Schools can convert class advantage into educational success.

moments.title: Reproduction in Education, Society and Culture
moments.body: Their book formalises 'symbolic violence' as the imposition of dominant culture as legitimate.
moments.takeaway: Domination operates through legitimation as well as force.

moments.title: Distinction
moments.body: Distinction maps French taste hierarchies onto class, with habitus mediating between class position and cultural preferences.
moments.takeaway: Taste is a structured field of class signalling.

now.title: Bourdieu in inequality research
now.body: Cultural capital underpins much sociology of education and stratification (e.g. Savage's Great British Class Survey).
now.open_questions: How does digital cultural capital map onto offline distinction?

items.reflection: Bourdieu insisted that empirical sociology requires both quantitative and ethnographic rigour.

moments.title: Schooling in Capitalist America
moments.body: Bowles and Gintis argue US schools reproduce class relations through a 'correspondence' between school discipline and workplace hierarchies.
moments.takeaway: Education's hidden curriculum aligns students with the labour market.

moments.title: Learning to Labour
moments.body: Willis's ethnography of West Midlands 'lads' shows working-class boys actively producing their own class trajectory through counter-school culture.
moments.takeaway: Reproduction is also active resistance.

moments.title: Bowles and Gintis revisit
moments.body: Their Sociology of Education paper revisits the correspondence thesis, qualifying it but defending core claims.
moments.takeaway: Major theses get revisited as labour markets change.

now.title: Schools and inequality
now.body: Sociology of education uses both correspondence-style and Bourdieusian frameworks, alongside policy-focused 'closing the gap' research.
now.open_questions: How does the rise of credential inflation alter the correspondence between schooling and work?

items.reflection: Bowles and Gintis's book remains in print because the question of what school is for remains open.

moments.title: Outsiders
moments.body: Becker argues deviance is created by social groups making rules whose infraction constitutes deviance.

quote.text: Deviance is not a quality of the act the person commits, but rather a consequence of the application by others of rules and sanctions to an 'offender'.

moments.takeaway: Labelling theory shifted deviance research from acts to processes.

moments.title: Primary and secondary deviance
moments.body: Lemert distinguishes primary deviance (initial rule breaking) from secondary deviance (deviance adopted as identity after labelling).
moments.takeaway: Labels can produce careers in deviance.

moments.title: Folk Devils and Moral Panics
moments.body: Cohen's study of mods and rockers introduces the moral panic concept to British sociology.
moments.takeaway: Media amplification can produce the deviance it reports.

now.title: Labelling in policy
now.body: Labelling theory informs critiques of school exclusion, gang databases and drug policy.
now.open_questions: How do online communities reshape labelling and counter-labelling?

items.reflection: Becker insisted sociology should ask whose side it was on.

moments.title: Delinquent Boys
moments.body: Cohen argues working-class boys, judged by middle-class school standards, experience status frustration and form delinquent subcultures.
moments.takeaway: Group-level adaptations to strain produce subcultures.

moments.title: Delinquency and Opportunity
moments.body: Cloward and Ohlin extend strain theory by examining differential access to illegitimate opportunity structures.
moments.takeaway: Crime is shaped by both legitimate and illegitimate opportunity.

moments.title: General Strain Theory
moments.body: Agnew broadens strain to include negative emotions arising from frustrated goals, loss and noxious stimuli.
moments.takeaway: Strain theory can be extended beyond economic goals.

now.title: Subculture studies today
now.body: Post-subcultural and neo-tribal theories question the stability of bounded subcultures, especially online.
now.open_questions: Are online deviant communities subcultures in Cohen's sense?

items.reflection: Cohen's framework moved sociology of deviance from individual pathology to collective adaptation.

moments.title: Some Principles of Stratification
moments.body: Davis and Moore argue inequality is functionally necessary to motivate talented individuals into important roles.
moments.takeaway: Functionalist stratification became sociology's most contested 1945 paper.

moments.title: Tumin critique
moments.body: Tumin argues Davis-Moore confuses motivation with necessity and underestimates how inequality blocks talent.
moments.takeaway: Internal critique kept stratification theory contested.

moments.title: Goldthorpe's mobility study
moments.body: Goldthorpe's study of 10,000 British men finds substantial absolute mobility but stable relative mobility.
moments.takeaway: Empirical mobility research grounded the abstract debate.

now.title: Stratification today
now.body: Modern stratification research uses occupational, cultural and wealth measures. Mobility data informs policy debates on opportunity.
now.open_questions: Has cross-generational mobility stalled in advanced economies?

items.reflection: Davis and Moore's article was short; the debate it provoked filled libraries.

moments.title: The Feminine Mystique
moments.body: Friedan names 'the problem that has no name', the dissatisfaction of educated suburban American housewives.

quote.text: The problem that has no name... is taking a far greater toll on the physical and mental health of our country than any known disease.

moments.takeaway: A book can name a structural condition and trigger a movement.

moments.title: National Organization for Women
moments.body: NOW is founded, channelling second-wave feminism into legal and political action.
moments.takeaway: Movements need organisations as well as ideas.

moments.title: The Second Stage
moments.body: Friedan reconsiders second-wave feminism's relationship to family and male-female partnership.
moments.takeaway: Movement leaders sometimes revisit their own framings.

now.title: Feminist sociology today
now.body: Black feminism, intersectionality, queer studies and gender studies have transformed feminist sociology since Friedan.
now.open_questions: How should sociology of gender integrate trans and non-binary perspectives?

items.reflection: Friedan's book was a New York Times bestseller for years and rewired American gender politics.

moments.title: Theorising Patriarchy
moments.body: Walby distinguishes six structures of patriarchy: household production, paid work, the state, male violence, sexuality and culture.
moments.takeaway: Patriarchy is multi-structural and historically variable.

moments.title: Gender Transformations
moments.body: Walby argues patriarchy has shifted from private to public form, integrating women into paid work while maintaining gender hierarchies.
moments.takeaway: Gender regimes change rather than disappear.

moments.title: Globalization and Inequalities
moments.body: Walby integrates gender, class, ethnicity and global structures into a complex-systems framework.
moments.takeaway: Gender analysis is reframed for a global economy.

now.title: Patriarchy across regimes
now.body: Walby's framework informs comparative research on gender regimes across welfare states and Global South contexts.
now.open_questions: How does the gig economy reshape Walby's six structures?

items.reflection: Walby kept patriarchy as a serious analytic category when many sociologists abandoned the term.

moments.title: Demarginalizing the Intersection
moments.body: Crenshaw introduces intersectionality through a critique of anti-discrimination law's inability to address Black women's claims.
moments.takeaway: Single-axis frameworks invisibilise compound disadvantage.

moments.title: Mapping the Margins
moments.body: Her Stanford Law Review article extends intersectionality to political and structural domains.
moments.takeaway: Intersectionality is both descriptive and political.

moments.title: Black Feminist Thought
moments.body: Collins's foundational work develops Black feminist standpoint epistemology.
moments.takeaway: Standpoint theory grounds intersectional analysis.

now.title: Intersectionality across sociology
now.body: Intersectionality is now mainstream in sociology of inequality, with active debates about its measurement and applications.
now.open_questions: How should quantitative sociology operationalise intersectionality?

items.reflection: Crenshaw's legal-theory term migrated into sociology and public discourse over three decades.

moments.title: The Philadelphia Negro
moments.who: W. E. B. Du Bois, Pennsylvania
moments.body: Du Bois conducts one of the first urban sociological studies in the US, documenting Philadelphia's Black community.
moments.takeaway: Du Bois's empirical sociology preceded the Chicago School.

moments.title: The Souls of Black Folk
moments.body: Du Bois develops 'double consciousness' and frames the 20th century around 'the problem of the color line'.

quote.text: The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color line.

moments.takeaway: Race becomes a category for sociological theory, not just description.

moments.title: ASA Du Bois centenary
moments.body: ASA acknowledges Du Bois's foundational role and his long marginalisation in disciplinary history.
moments.takeaway: Disciplinary canon revision continues.

now.title: Race in sociology
now.body: Critical race theory, racialisation and whiteness studies all engage Du Bois's foundational framing.
now.open_questions: How should sociology address racial categories in countries with different histories of racial classification?

items.reflection: Du Bois's 95-year career spanned the founding of American sociology and the civil rights era.

moments.title: Encoding/decoding paper
moments.body: Hall argues media messages are encoded with preferred meanings but decoded by audiences in dominant, negotiated or oppositional ways.
moments.takeaway: Media meaning is the outcome of an encounter, not a one-way transmission.

moments.title: Policing the Crisis
moments.body: A collective study of mugging and moral panic in 1970s Britain links race, crime reporting and the politics of authoritarian populism.
moments.takeaway: Cultural studies integrated political-economic analysis.

moments.title: Representation
moments.body: Hall's edited collection sets out the constructionist approach to representation that shapes media studies curricula.
moments.takeaway: Edited collections shape teaching.

now.title: Cultural studies in digital media
now.body: Hall's frameworks remain central to studies of platforms, news and identity. Audience studies have moved into data-driven analysis.
now.open_questions: How does algorithmic mediation change Hall's encoding/decoding model?

items.reflection: Hall built Birmingham CCCS into the most influential cultural studies institution of the late 20th century.

moments.title: The Constitution of Society
moments.body: Giddens's structuration theory argues structure and agency are mutually constituted, with the 'duality of structure'.
moments.takeaway: Structuration theory aimed to dissolve the structure-agency dichotomy.

moments.title: The Consequences of Modernity
moments.body: Giddens characterises late modernity through time-space distanciation, disembedding and reflexivity.
moments.takeaway: Modernity is a distinctive social form, not just continuity from tradition.

moments.title: The Third Way
moments.body: Giddens's policy book influences Blair's New Labour and centre-left politics across Europe.
moments.takeaway: Social theory can directly shape political practice.

now.title: Modernity and risk
now.body: Giddens's frameworks coexist with Beck's risk society and Bauman's liquid modernity in contemporary theory.
now.open_questions: Does climate change require a different theory of modernity?

items.reflection: Giddens combined high theory with public-intellectual reach more than any UK sociologist of his generation.

moments.title: Risk Society
moments.body: Beck's book is published shortly after Chernobyl. Modern society, he argues, produces manufactured risks that overflow national and class boundaries.
moments.takeaway: Risk reorganises social conflict.

moments.title: English translation
moments.body: Beck's book reaches anglophone sociology, shaping debates about globalisation and the environment.
moments.takeaway: Translation timing again reshapes a thinker's audience.

moments.title: Individualization
moments.body: Beck and Beck-Gernsheim analyse how individualisation reorganises family, biography and work.
moments.takeaway: Risk society implies new biographical structures.

now.title: Risk in global perspective
now.body: Pandemics, climate change and AI risks are analysed through Beck's framework, alongside critiques of its Eurocentric assumptions.
now.open_questions: How does Beck's framework apply to societies experiencing climate risk before late modernity?

items.reflection: Beck's book transformed environmental sociology and modern political theory.

moments.title: Modernity and the Holocaust
moments.body: Bauman argues the Holocaust was not a deviation from modernity but a possibility built into modern bureaucratic rationality.
moments.takeaway: Modernity's dark side cannot be exorcised.

moments.title: Liquid Modernity
moments.body: Bauman characterises contemporary modernity as 'liquid', with melting institutions and individualised biographies.
moments.takeaway: Stability gives way to ongoing reconstitution.

moments.title: Liquid Love
moments.body: Bauman extends liquid modernity to intimate relationships in a series of accessible books.
moments.takeaway: Public sociology can sustain a prolific career.

now.title: Liquid modernity in digital society
now.body: Bauman's frameworks are used to analyse precarious work, online identity and consumerist subjectivity.
now.open_questions: Are platform societies more 'liquid' or more 'crystallised' than Bauman's late-20th-century cases?

items.reflection: Bauman wrote dozens of books in his last two decades, building a public sociology readership.

moments.title: The Gutenberg Galaxy
moments.body: McLuhan analyses the transition from oral to print culture and predicts an electronic 'global village'.
moments.takeaway: Media shape cognition and social organisation.

moments.title: Understanding Media
moments.body: McLuhan's aphoristic book introduces 'the medium is the message' and the distinction between hot and cool media.
moments.takeaway: Form of media is more important than content.

moments.title: The Global Village
moments.body: Co-authored with Bruce Powers and published after McLuhan's death, the book restates his thesis for the early internet era.
moments.takeaway: Theorists' frames sometimes anticipate technologies they did not see.

now.title: McLuhan online
now.body: Digital sociology revisits McLuhan as platforms reshape attention, news and politics.
now.open_questions: Are platforms a new 'hot' medium or do they require new categories?

items.reflection: McLuhan's reputation has cycled in and out of academic respectability since the 1960s.

moments.title: The Rise of the Network Society
moments.body: Castells argues information technology produces a new mode of development based on networks and flows.
moments.takeaway: Network society replaces industrial society as the master frame.

moments.title: End of Millennium
moments.body: The third volume of his Information Age trilogy charts the collapse of Soviet statism, the rise of the Pacific economy and the emergence of a Fourth World of excluded populations.
moments.takeaway: Network society includes its own forms of exclusion.

moments.title: Networks of Outrage and Hope
moments.body: Castells analyses the 2011 movements (Arab Spring, Indignados, Occupy) as network-mediated mobilisations.
moments.takeaway: Networked protest is theorised in real time.

now.title: Platform society
now.body: Subsequent theorists (van Dijck, Srnicek) extend Castells into the era of platform capitalism.
now.open_questions: Are platforms the highest form of network society or a different regime?

items.reflection: Castells's 1,500-page trilogy is one of the most ambitious sociological works of the late 20th century.

moments.title: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
moments.body: Weber links Calvinist asceticism and the 'calling' to dispositions favourable to capital accumulation.
moments.takeaway: Religion can shape economic behaviour.

moments.title: The Sacred Canopy
moments.body: Berger argues religion provides a 'sacred canopy' of meaning, and that modernity erodes it.
moments.takeaway: Secularisation was treated as a near-inevitability.

moments.title: The Desecularization of the World
moments.body: Berger publicly revises his secularisation thesis, acknowledging the global resurgence of religion.
moments.takeaway: Even leading theorists revise their predictions.

now.title: Religion and modernity
now.body: Sociology of religion now examines multiple modernities, Pentecostalism, post-secularism and religious nationalism.
now.open_questions: How does religious adherence relate to politics in post-secular democracies?

items.reflection: Weber's link between religion and economic action remains contested but unavoidable.

moments.title: Cultivation theory
moments.body: Gerbner's cultural indicators project argues heavy television viewing 'cultivates' a 'mean world' view.
moments.takeaway: Cumulative exposure can shape perceptions of social reality.

moments.title: Living with Television
moments.body: The cultivation framework is extended to mainstreaming and resonance effects.
moments.takeaway: Cultivation theory matures as a research programme.

moments.title: Meta-analysis of cultivation
moments.body: Their meta-analysis finds small but persistent cultivation effects across decades of studies.
moments.takeaway: Effects can be small but cumulative.

now.title: Cultivation in algorithmic media
now.body: Cultivation logic is applied to social media exposure, news consumption and platform recommendation.
now.open_questions: How does fragmented digital exposure affect cultivation processes?

items.reflection: Gerbner's framework offered a middle ground between strong-effects and limited-effects media theory.

moments.title: Awareness of Dying
moments.body: Their hospital study of awareness contexts in dying produces both findings and a methodological example.
moments.takeaway: Method emerges from empirical practice.

moments.title: The Discovery of Grounded Theory
moments.body: Their book formalises grounded theory as an alternative to grand theory and verificationist quantitative work.
moments.takeaway: A methodology can democratise theory building.

moments.title: Glaser-Strauss split
moments.body: Strauss and Juliet Corbin develop a more proceduralised grounded theory; Glaser objects.
moments.takeaway: Methodologies branch as they spread.

now.title: Grounded theory today
now.body: Constructivist grounded theory (Charmaz) and pragmatist variants dominate contemporary qualitative method teaching.
now.open_questions: How should grounded theory be combined with computational text analysis?

items.reflection: Glaser and Strauss made qualitative method respectable in a discipline turning quantitative.

moments.title: Ethnic Minorities in Britain
moments.body: The fourth PSI survey of ethnic minorities documents diversity of outcomes across British ethnic groups.
moments.takeaway: Ethnic minorities are heterogeneous in outcomes.

moments.title: Multicultural Politics
moments.body: Modood defends a 'moderate secularist' multiculturalism that includes religion alongside ethnicity.
moments.takeaway: Multiculturalism is reframed for a post-9/11 era.

moments.title: Multiculturalism revisited
moments.body: Edited volumes defend multiculturalism against the 'failure of multiculturalism' political narrative.
moments.takeaway: Public-policy debates feed back into sociological theory.

now.title: Ethnicity in policy and theory
now.body: Race and ethnicity research increasingly engages religion, citizenship and intersectional inequality.
now.open_questions: How should sociology integrate religion as a category alongside race?

items.reflection: Modood reframed UK race and ethnicity research to take religion seriously.

moments.title: Black Lives Matter founded
moments.body: BLM begins as a hashtag after the acquittal of George Zimmerman in the killing of Trayvon Martin.
moments.takeaway: A hashtag can seed a movement.

moments.title: Ferguson protests
moments.body: Protests in Ferguson, Missouri after the killing of Michael Brown bring BLM to national prominence.
moments.takeaway: Local events catalyse national mobilisation.

moments.title: George Floyd protests
moments.body: The killing of George Floyd in May 2020 produces the largest US protests in modern history and global solidarity actions.
moments.takeaway: Movements scale globally when digital infrastructure aligns with local grievance.

now.title: Race, policing and movements
now.body: Sociology engages BLM via social movements theory, racial capitalism, and policing research.
now.open_questions: What institutional change has BLM produced in policing and education?

items.reflection: BLM is the most-studied US social movement of the 21st century to date.

moments.title: Learning to Labour
moments.body: Willis's ethnography follows 12 working-class 'lads' through their final years of school in the West Midlands and into the factory.
moments.takeaway: Working-class boys actively produce their own class trajectory through counter-school culture.

moments.title: Beachside Comprehensive
moments.body: Ball's ethnography of a Sussex comprehensive school documents the interaction of streaming and class background.
moments.takeaway: School-level processes shape educational outcomes.

moments.title: Crisis in the Classroom?
moments.body: Sociology of education debates the legacy of Willis and the meaning of class for educational reproduction in the 1980s.
moments.takeaway: The Willis legacy was contested as quickly as it was established.

now.title: Class and education today
now.body: Contemporary sociology of education combines Bourdieusian and Willis-style frameworks with attention to gender, race and migration.
now.open_questions: What does a counter-school culture look like in the era of platform work?

items.reflection: Willis turned a small qualitative sample into one of British sociology's most cited studies.

moments.title: Ain't I a Woman
moments.body: hooks's first book challenges the centring of white middle-class women in second-wave feminism.
moments.takeaway: Black feminist critique reframes feminist theory.

moments.title: Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center
moments.body: hooks argues feminist theory must start from the experience of those at the margins of multiple systems of domination.
moments.takeaway: Standpoint shifts who counts as theorist.

moments.title: All About Love
moments.body: hooks moves into accessible writing on love, masculinity and education for a broader audience.
moments.takeaway: Public sociology builds different audiences.

now.title: Feminist theory and intersectionality
now.body: hooks's writing remains a core resource for intersectional, anti-racist and feminist pedagogy.
now.open_questions: How should feminist sociology integrate care, love and emotional labour?

items.reflection: hooks deliberately lower-cased her name to centre ideas over identity; her death in 2021 was widely marked.

moments.title: The Death of Class
moments.body: Pakulski and Waters argue economic class has lost its centrality in shaping life chances and identity, displaced by status and consumption.
moments.takeaway: Postmodern theorists contested class's continuing relevance.

moments.title: The Class debate
moments.body: British class analysts defend the centrality of class through empirical mobility and inequality data.
moments.takeaway: Empirical evidence is mobilised in theoretical disputes.

moments.title: Great British Class Survey
moments.body: BBC-collected data yields a seven-class schema combining economic, cultural and social capital.
moments.takeaway: Bourdieusian frameworks regenerate class analysis.

now.title: Class in 21st-century sociology
now.body: Class returned to the centre of British sociology after 2008 inequality debates and Brexit.
now.open_questions: How does class intersect with race, region and generation in 21st-century stratification?

items.reflection: The 'death of class' proved premature; the conditions for its return were already gathering.

moments.title: Discipline and Punish
moments.body: Foucault traces the shift from spectacular punishment to disciplinary techniques aimed at producing docile bodies.
moments.takeaway: Power operates through visibility, classification and routine.

moments.title: History of Sexuality, Volume 1
moments.body: Foucault challenges the 'repressive hypothesis' and analyses biopower as the management of populations.
moments.takeaway: Sex was incited as a category, not just repressed.

moments.title: Lectures on governmentality
moments.body: Foucault introduces governmentality, broadening his analysis to liberalism and neoliberalism.
moments.takeaway: Power is theorised as conduct of conduct.

now.title: Foucault in surveillance studies
now.body: Foucauldian analysis of surveillance, biopolitics and governmentality is widespread in sociology, criminology and political theory.
now.open_questions: What new forms of governmentality does platform infrastructure enable?

items.reflection: Foucault's lectures were attended in their hundreds; the College de France recordings now structure his reception.

moments.title: Making Democracy Work
moments.body: Putnam's study of Italian regional government links institutional performance to social capital.
moments.takeaway: Social capital is operationalised as a measurable variable.

moments.title: Bowling Alone article
moments.body: Putnam's Journal of Democracy article documents declining civic engagement in the US.
moments.takeaway: Civic decline becomes a measurable trend.

moments.title: Bowling Alone book
moments.body: The book documents a broad decline in associational membership and proposes bridging and bonding capital as distinct forms.
moments.takeaway: Bridging social capital ties together heterogeneous communities.

now.title: Social capital after Putnam
now.body: Critics question the causal claims; the framework remains central to social policy, public health and education research.
now.open_questions: Has online sociability replaced or merely shifted offline civic engagement?

items.reflection: Putnam's book reached US presidents and shaped two decades of community policy.
